text: ABSTRACT
section: Thermodynamic aspects of bis(3‑sulfopropyl) disulfide and 3‑mercapto‑1‑propanesulfonic acid in Cu electrodeposition > ABSTRACT

text: Organic additives play an important role in regulating fi lm growth and properties in Cu electrodeposition. 3‑Mercapto‑1‑propane sulfonate (MPS) and its dimer bis(3‑sulfopropyl) disulfide (SPS) are representative accelerators that promote Cu electrodeposition rate. In this study, the formal reduction potential of SPS to MPS wa determined by measuring the equilibrium constants of thiol–disulfide interchange reactions with the reference thiol/disul fi de pairs by 1 H nuclear magnetic resonance (1H NMR) spectroscopy. The calculated formal reduction potential of SPS to MPS was 0.153 V (vs. standard hydrogen electrode). Based on this calculation, the cell potentials of Cu(I)(thiolate) formation reaction with either SPS or MPS, which is a key reaction in accelerating mechanism, were also estimated by ultraviolet–visible absorption and 1 H NMR spectroscopies: they were found to be 0.202 V and 0.214 V for SPS and MPS, respectively. The positive cell potential indicates that the formation of Cu(I)(thiolate) complexes is thermodynamically favorable in the presence of additives.

text: 1. Introduction
section: Thermodynamic aspects of bis(3‑sulfopropyl) disulfide and 3‑mercapto‑1‑propanesulfonic acid in Cu electrodeposition > 1. Introduction

text: Cu has been widely used as metallization material in the semi conductor industry owing to its low electrical resistivity and high electromigration resistance. Cu metallization is usually performed by electrodeposition, which e fi ciently yields high quality fi lms by a relatively simple and inexpensive process. Electrolyte for Cu electrodeposition typically contains small quantities of organic additives, which are essential to regulate fi lm growth and properties. Additives are grouped into accelerators, suppressors, and levelers according to their roles in controlling the deposition rate. Among them, 3‑mercap to‑1‑propanesulfonate (MPS) and its dimer bis(3‑sulfopropyl) disulfide (SPS) are the most representative accelerators in Cu electrodeposition [1].
section: Thermodynamic aspects of bis(3‑sulfopropyl) disulfide and 3‑mercapto‑1‑propanesulfonic acid in Cu electrodeposition > 1. Introduction

text: The accelerating e f ect of SPS or MPS has been explained by two mechanisms [2]. One describes competitive adsorption between accel erator and suppressor; the displacement of suppressor inhibition layer by SPS or MPS facilitates the approach of Cu ions to electrode surface, enhancing the deposition rate [ 3 - 7 ]. The other mechanism focuses on direct catalytic reduction of Cu ^2 + ion to C u ^+ ion by forming Cu(I) (thiolate) complex [8–11]. The reduction of Cu ^2 + to Cu ^+ is known as the rate-determining step of Cu electrodeposition [12]. Vereecken et al. reported that the amount of C u ^+ near electrode surface is a key factor determining the deposition rate in Cu electrodeposition [13,14].

MPS or SPS in electrolyte can form stable Cu(I)(thiolate) complex, increasing the amount of C u ^+ species near the electrode surface [14]. The corresponding reactions are described as follows.

The formal reduction potential of SPS was obtained by measuring the chemical equilibrium constants of thiol–disulfide interchange reaction between MPS/SPS pairs and reference thiol/disul fi de pairs, lipoic acid (Lip) and mercaptoethanol (ME). The calculation provides thermodynamic information of accelerating mechanism by either SPS or MPS in Cu electrodeposition.

text: 2.1. Electrochemical analysis
section: Thermodynamic aspects of bis(3‑sulfopropyl) disulfide and 3‑mercapto‑1‑propanesulfonic acid in Cu electrodeposition > 2.1. Electrochemical analysis

text: Linear sweep voltammetry (LSV) was performed with electrolyte composed of 0.25 M CuSO and 1.0 M H SO. SPS or MPS was also added to the electrolyte. The concentrations of SPS and MPS were 50 μM and 100 μM, respectively, at which the equivalent concentration of thiolate functional group is same: one SPS is reduced to two MPS (Eq. (3)). The electrochemical analysis was conducted in a three-electrode system comprising a Cu rotating disk electrode ( 0.2 \thinspace cm ^2), Cu rod, and Ag / AgCl, /saturated KCl electrode ( Ag/AgCl) as the working electrode, the counter electrode, and the reference electrode, respectively. Temperature was held at 30^°C (303 K) by thermostat during the analysis. The potential applied on the working electrode was swept from 0.15 V to - 0.8 5 : V (vs. Ag/AgCl) at a scan rate of 10 mV/s using a potentiostat (PAR 273A, EG&G Princeton Applied Research Corporation). All the LSV analysis was conducted right after the solution preparation to minimize the extent of reactions, Eqs. (1) and (2).

text: 3.1. Electrochemical analysis of acceleration efect by SPS or MPS
section: Thermodynamic aspects of bis(3‑sulfopropyl) disulfide and 3‑mercapto‑1‑propanesulfonic acid in Cu electrodeposition > 3.1. Electrochemical analysis of acceleration efect by SPS or MPS

text: The accelerating e f ect of SPS or MPS in Cu electrodeposition was observed in LSV, as shown in Fig. 1. The addition of either SPS or MPS into deposition electrolyte increases Cu ion reduction current, indicating that the electrodeposition process is accelerated by direct catalytic reduction of Cu ^2 + to C u ^+ via formation of Cu(I)(thiolate) complex. It is notable that MPS exhibits slightly stronger acceleration e f ect than SPS at the same equivalent thiolate concentration, because MPS directly forms Cu(I)(thiolate) complex with major Cu ^2 +, whereas SPS only combines with minor C u ^+, coming from the comproportio nation reaction between Cu ^2 + and metallic Cu (Eq. (4)).

text: As a pair of thiol/disul fi de, SPS and MPS can react with another thiol/disulfide pair via substitution, which is called thiol–disulfide interchange reaction [19–22]. The reduction potential of disulfide compound in thiol–disulfide interchange is usually obtained by establishing the equilibrium between the target material and a reference thiol/disul fi de pair of known redox potential, rather than electroanalytical measurements because many redox systems of sulfur are electrochemically irreversible [ 1 5, 1 7, 2 3, 2 4 ]. The irreversible characteristic leads to the unsteady electrode potential which is inconsistent with the Nernst equation, hindering the accurate calculation of reduction potential. Therefore, in this study, the thiol–disulfide interchange reaction was introduced with Lip and ME as the reference materials. The thiol–disulfide interchange reactions between SPS/MPS and Lip/ME are as follows.

text: Fig. 4(a) shows the absorption spectra of a mixture of MPS and Cu ^ 2 + ions. The typical absorption band of Cu ^ 2 + ions is located between 700 nm and 900 nm, whereas MPS alone shows negligible absorption. A strong absorption peak in the range 300–450 nm was observed in the presence of both MPS and Cu^2+ ions with a signi fi cant decrease in the absorption by Cu ^ 2 + ions (700–900 nm). This peak is related to Cu(I) (thiolate) formed by the reaction between Cu^2+ and MPS via Eq. (1). In this reaction, the oxidative dimerization of MPS to SPS in the presence of Cu ^ 2 + leads to the formation of Cu(I)(thiolate) complex. It has been reported that the oxidative dimerization of MPS reduces Cu ^ 2 + to C u ^ + simultaneously and the reduction product ( Cu ^ +) form Cu(I)(thiolate) complex with either MPS or SPS [ 1 0, 2 6 ]. In contrast, SPS rarely forms Cu(I)(thiolate) complex with Cu ^ 2 +; the UV–vis spectrum of a mixture of Cu ^ 2 + and SPS is just a simple sum of each spectrum of Cu ^ 2 + and SPS (Fig. 4(b)). This result corresponds well with the observation by G. Cardona et al. [18]. SPS forms Cu(I)(thiolate) complex with C u ^ + instead.

text: the dissolution of a considerable amount of CuCl was observed in the presence of either MPS or SPS, because of the formation of Cu(I) (thiolate) complexes. These results support that MPS is able to form Cu (I)(thiolate) complex with both Cu ^2 + and C u ^+, whereas SPS forms the complex with only C u ^+ In the conventional CuSO –based Cu electrodeposition solution, major Cu species in the electrolyte is Cu ^2 +, not C u ^+. At this situation, there are two possible mechanisms for the formation of Cu(I)(thiolate) in the presence of SPS. One is that SPS is reduced to MPS and then reacts with Cu ^2 + +. The other mechanism proposes that SPS forms Cu(I) (thiolate) complex with C u ^+ formed via Eq. (4). However, many studies have shown that Cu(I)(thiolate) complex is formed via the latter mechanism, rather than the former [8,14]. Our UV–vis spectroscopy study also showed the same result (Fig. 4(e)). When CuSO_4 solution was mixed with the equivalent concentration of SPS in the presence of Cu foil fragment (2 mm × 2 mm), a strong absorption was observed in the range between 300 nm and 450 nm, related to Cu(I)(thiolate).

text: 4. Conclusions
section: Thermodynamic aspects of bis(3‑sulfopropyl) disulfide and 3‑mercapto‑1‑propanesulfonic acid in Cu electrodeposition > 4. Conclusions

text: The formal reduction potential of SPS was fi rst determined by using thiol–disulfide interchange reaction with ME and Lip. The calculated formal reduction potential of SPS under the standard condition was 0.153 V (vs. SHE) in aqueous solution. The cell potential of the formation of Cu(I)(thiolate) complexes, which is the key reaction to explain the accelerating mechanism, was also estimated based on the formal reduction potential of SPS. The cell potential of Cu(I)(thiolate) formation between C u ^+ and SPS was 0.202 V, and the reaction between Cu ^2 + and MPS was 0.214 V. We believe that the thermodynamic values obtained in this study would be helpful in understanding or developing industrial Cu electrodeposition involving SPS.
